subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Climate Change and Coffee
description: A 60-second lesson on Climate Change and Coffee.

hook.text: Rising temperatures are pushing arabica coffee toward extinction in the wild by 2080, scientists warn.

buildup.text: Arabica needs cool nights and steady rain. Even 1°C of warming increases pest pressure and reduces yield.

discovery.text: Farmers are moving plantations uphill, but mountains have peaks. Eventually, there's nowhere left to go.

twist.text: Wild coffee species like C. stenophylla taste like arabica but tolerate higher heat. They may be the answer.

climax.text: Breeding programs cross wild species with arabica to create heat-tolerant varieties that still taste good.

punchline.text: Coffee's future depends on genes from its wild past.

quiz.question: Why are wild coffee species important for the future?
options: They may provide heat-tolerant genes for breeding

details.summary: Climate change threatens to cut the land suitable for arabica production by up to 50 percent by 2050. Rising temperatures, erratic rainfall, and expanding pest ranges are already reducing yields and quality.
details.whyItMatters: Climate change could fundamentally alter what coffee is available, where it comes from, and how much it costs within a generation.
takeaways: Suitable arabica land could shrink 50 percent by 2050
Temperature rise increases pest pressure and reduces quality
Climate-resilient breeding programs are urgently needed

faq.question: Which coffee-producing regions are most threatened?
faq.answer: Low-altitude growing areas in Brazil, Central America, Vietnam, and parts of East Africa face the most immediate threat. Ethiopia's wild coffee forests, which hold irreplaceable genetic diversity, are also highly vulnerable. No major producing region is immune.

faq.question: What can be done to save coffee from climate change?
faq.answer: Research institutions are breeding heat-tolerant varieties that retain flavor quality. Farmers are adopting shade trees, water conservation, and agroforestry. Moving production to higher altitudes is occurring naturally. Reducing carbon emissions remains the most impactful long-term solution.
